title: Team Members Who Sugar-Coat Their Feedback to Colleagues
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece tackles the challenge of getting conflict-averse team members to give honest feedback instead of relentlessly positive spin. Rather than relying solely on anonymous feedback tools, which the author considers a weak substitute, the recommended approach is asking pointed questions that are hard to sidestep, such as what one thing a colleague could change to improve. The article acknowledges that even reluctant peers will try to dodge these questions by claiming they can't think of anything, and instructs leaders to keep pushing rather than accept that answer. The piece frames this as a leader's job: engineering the conditions for candor rather than hoping for it.
points: Some team members avoid honest criticism to preserve social harmony and avoid uncomfortable conversations
Anonymous feedback tools can help but are a poor substitute for genuine peer candor
Specific, hard-to-dodge questions (what one thing could they change?) draw out more honest answers
Leaders should keep pushing past the I can't think of anything deflection rather than accept it
quotes: Team members who prioritize being liked, projecting positivity, and showing support for their colleagues will often sugar-coat their feedback and refrain from truthful criticism.
So, when asked for feedback, they pull their punches and highlight only the positives as a way to maintain social harmony and to avoid damaging their relationships.
The best leaders know a secret. Under the right questioning, even feedback-evasive team members will offer more candid views to their colleagues.
These questions are difficult to duck or dismiss, although the most reluctant peers will still find a way to avoid them, usually by claiming they can’t think of an answer.
Good leaders don’t accept this Texas two-step. They push for a more constructive answer anyway.
